# Relative Error of Scaled Poisson Approximation via Stein’s Method

**Authors:** Yingdong Lu Address: IBM Research Email address: yingdong@us.ibm.com , Yue Tan Address: Ohio State University Email address: tan.268@buckeyemail.osu.edu and Cathy H. Xia Address: Ohio State University Email address: xia.52@osu.edu

## Abstract

We study the accuracy of a scaled Poisson approximation to the weighted sum of independent Poisson random variables, focusing on in particular the relative error of the tail distribution. A bound on the relative approximation error is established using a modified Stein-Chen method.

## 1. Introduction

Weighted summation of independent Poisson random variables (r.v.s) is a probabilistic entity that plays a crucial role in a wide variety of applications, such as epidemiology [12], physics [5], and computer science [23]. A traditional approach of its quantification is a normal approximation matching the first two moments, which can be effective when the mean is large. In [14], a scaled Poisson approximation that matches the first two moments after a scaling is proposed. That is, the distribution of $S$ , a weighted sum of independent Poisson random variables with mean $\mu=E[S]$ and variance $\sigma^{2}=Var(S)$ , is approximated by that of a scaled Poisson random variable, i.e.,

$$ S\approx_{d}\frac{1}{\beta}A_{\beta\mu},\quad\quad\quad\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}, $$

where $A_{\lambda}$ denotes a Poisson r.v. with mean $\lambda$ . This way, the first two moments of $S$ are matched by that of the approximation. Through numerical experiments, [14] reports that this approach produces a more accurate tail approximation than the normal approximation. Moreover, the approximation is often more conservative which serves certain types of application well, see, e.g. [14, 19, 22]. However, no theoretical analysis on the quality of this approximation has been given nor is the approximation error well understood. It is the purpose of this paper to address these issues by providing quantitative bounds on the relative error of this approximation, utilizing a novel application of the Stein method.

The Stein’s method has been a powerful tool for bounding the error of an approximating distribution to an unknown distribution. The method was first introduced by Charles Stein [21] to study the normal approximation to the distribution of a sum of dependent r.v.’s. It was later extended to handle Poisson approximations in [9], often referred to as the Stein-Chen method specifically for studying Poisson approximations. The Stein’s method has been used to study many approximating distributions including binomial distribution [13], multinomial distribution [17], compound Poisson distribution [2], Gamma distribution [18], geometric distribution [20], etc. Applications in other contexts include [8], [24], [15], [11], [7], and [6].

The Stein’s method relies on identifying a Stein’s operator $\mathcal{A}$ associated with a given distribution $Q$ such that a r.v. $Y$ follows distribution $Q$ (written as $Y\sim Q$ ) if and only if $E(\mathcal{A}f)(Y)=0$ for all bounded real-valued functions $f$ defined on the range of $Y$ . If the distribution of a r.v. $W$ can be well approximated by $Q$ , then $E(\mathcal{A}f)(W)\approx 0$ . The error of approximating $E[h(W)]$ by $E[h(Y)]$ , for a given metric function $h$ , can then be estimated by studying the behavior of $E\mathcal{A}f_{h}(W)$ . where $f_{h}$ is a solution to the so-called Stein’s equation:

$$ \mathcal{A}f(w)=h(w)-Eh(Y). $$

The Stein’s operator $\mathcal{A}$ frequently used in studying Poisson approximations was provided by [9] and often referred to as the Stein-Chen method:

$$ \mathcal{A}f(w)=\lambda\cdot f(w+1)-wf(w), $$

Using the Stein-Chen method, moderate deviation bounds on the relative error of a Poisson approximation to a summation of locally dependent indicators was established in [10], and were later made more general and explicit in [16].

For the scaled Poisson approximation (1), the scalar $\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}$ is typically not integer-valued, thus the conventional Stein’s operator $\mathcal{A}$ given by (3) can not be applied directly as it only acts on bounded functions $f$ defined on the integers. We show that, when the scalar is a rational number with $\beta=\frac{n}{m}$ , the scaled Poisson approximation (1), now equivalent to $nS\approx mA_{\lambda}$ with $\lambda=\beta\mu$ , can still be analyzed via the Stein’s method. We introduce a new Stein’s operator for $\hat{A}_{\lambda}:=mA_{\lambda}$ , defined as:

$$ \mathcal{A}f(w)=\lambda mf(w+m)-wf(w), $$

which provides a more suitable framework for studying the approximation. This requires us to obtain new solutions to this Stein’s equation and study the quantitative properties of the solution, which form the most technical part of the paper. These properties allow us to apply Stein’s method and derive bound on the relative error of scaled Poisson approximation. We then extend our relative error bound to the case when $\beta$ is irrational using bounded convergence theorem.

We emphasize that while the scaled Poisson approximation has been widely used in practice, to the best our knowledge, this is the first work to quantify the relative error of the approximation via moderate deviations bound. Meanwhile, the scaled Stein method provides a new method for analyzing approximations on a grid with applications beyond the weighted Poisson summation discussed in this paper. Moreover, the techniques developed in estimating differences of the solutions to the Stein’s equations appeared to reveal some fundamental properties of Poisson distribution function, should be of independent interests.

Our bound on the relative error is similar in spirit and numerically comparable to those obtained in [16] for (non-scaled) Poisson approximation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that one of the conjectures raised in [16] is valid beyond a threshold for which we provide an explicit expression.

The rest of the paper is organized as follow. In Section 2, we present the main results of the paper, which include a new Stein’s operator, our relative error bound for the scaled Poisson approximation, and a proposition to address one of the conjectures raised in [16]. Proof for the main results is presented in Section 3; Key properties of the solution to modified Stein’s equation are collected in Section 4. The paper is concluded in Section 5 with summary and ongoing research.

## 2. Main Results and Implications

In this section, we present the problem of scaled Poisson approximation, the main results and their implications. Assumptions of the scaled Poisson approximation are presented in Sec. 2.1; a modified Stein’s method is introduced in Sec. 2.2; and our moderate deviations result is elaborated in Sec. 2.3.

### 2.1. Scaled Poisson Approximation

Consider a weighted summation of $R$ independent Poisson r.v.s $\{A_{\nu_{r}}\}_{r=1}^{R}$ ,

$$ S:=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}, $$

where $A_{\nu}$ denotes a Poisson random variable with mean $\nu$ and $\{b_{r}\}_{r=1}^{R}$ are a set of positive weights. Without loss of generality, we assume that $b_{r}$ ’s are distinct and $0<b_{1}<b_{2}<\cdots<b_{R}$ . If there exist $r$ and $s$ such that $b_{r}=b_{s}$ , one can simply merge the two classes into one as $b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}+b_{s}A_{\nu_{s}}\overset{d}{=}b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}+\nu_{s}}$ .

Denote the mean and variance of $S$ as $\mu=E[S]$ , and $\sigma^{2}=Var(S)$ respectively, thus,

$$ \mu=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}\nu_{r},\quad\quad\sigma^{2}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}^{2}\nu_{r}. $$

Let $\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}$ , which is known as the inverse of dispersion index.

We consider a scaled Poisson approximation to $S$ , i.e. $S\approx_{d}\frac{1}{\beta}A_{\beta\mu}$ , as introduced in (1). It can be easily verified that the first two moments of $S$ are matched by that of the approximation. We focus on deriving moderate derivations results on the relative error of the tail distributions.

In order to utilize the Stein-Chen method to compare the two distributions, which only works for integers, we first make the following assumption. We show later our relative error bound also holds without the assumption.

#### Assumption 1.

Assume that the weights $b_{r}$ ’s are positive integers, and $\beta$ is rational and can be expressed as $\beta=\frac{n}{m}$ where $n$ and $m$ are relatively prime.

In some applications such as those in [22], Assumption 1 holds naturally. Under Assumption 1, the scaled Poisson approximation can be rewritten as

$$ nS\approx_{d}\hat{A}_{\lambda},\quad\mbox{ where }\hat{A}_{\lambda}:=mA_{\lambda},\mbox{ and }\lambda=\beta\mu. $$

Note that both $nS$ and $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ are now integer-valued r.v.s.

### 2.2. Stein’s Method for Scaled Poisson Random Variable

We next present a modified Stein’s method that will help establish moderate deviations results on the tail distributions under approximation (7). Note that the conventional Stein’s operator $\mathcal{A}$ given by (3) no longer works for $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ , since it is a scaled Poisson random variable that only takes values on grid $m\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , where $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ denotes the set of nonnegative integers. The next Lemma establishes the Stein’s operator for $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ . Its proof can be found in Appendix A.

#### Lemma 2.1.

The Stein’s operator for $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ is

$$ \mathcal{A}f(w):=\lambda mf(w+m)-wf(w). $$

That is, $E(\mathcal{A}f)(\hat{A}_{\lambda})=0$ for all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $Z_{\geq 0}$ .

For a given metric function $h(\cdot)$ , the Stein’s equation for $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ bears the following form,

$$ \mathcal{A}f(w)=\lambda mf(w+m)-wf(w)=h(w)-Eh(\hat{A}_{\lambda}). $$

The following Lemma provides a representation of $f_{h}$ , the solution to Stein’s equation (9), which will be useful in establishing our moderate deviations results. The proof can be found in Appendix B.

#### Lemma 2.2.

The following form

$$ f_{h}(w)=-\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}[h(w+mj)-Eh({\hat{A}}_{\lambda})] $$

is a solution to the Stein’s equation (9).

Based on (9), the difference $E[h(nS)]-E[h({\hat{A}}_{\lambda})]$ can then be estimated, by studying $E\mathcal{A}f_{h}(nS)=E[\lambda mf(nS+m)-nSf(nS)]$ . The following lemmas provide keys to such estimations.

#### Lemma 2.3.

For any bounded function $f(\cdot)$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle E[nSf(nS)]= \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{R}nb_{r}\nu_{r}E\left[f\left(nS+nb_{r}\right)\right]=m\lambda\sum_{r=1}^{R}\delta_{r}E\left[f\left(nS+nb_{r}\right)\right], $$

where $\delta_{r}=\frac{b_{r}\nu_{r}}{\mu}$ , and $\sum_{r=1}^{R}\delta_{r}=1$ .

Proof can be found in Appendix C. The following lemma is then immediate.

#### Lemma 2.4.

$$ E(\mathcal{A}f_{h})(nS)=\lambda mE[f(nS+m)]-E[nSf(nS)]=H_{1}+\cdots+H_{R}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle H_{r} \displaystyle=m\lambda\delta_{r}E[(f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+nb_{r})],\quad r=1,\dots,R. $$

Based on (6), we can write

$$ \frac{1}{\beta}=\frac{m}{n}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\mu}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}\frac{b_{r}\nu_{r}}{\mu}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}\delta_{r}. $$

That is, $m=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\delta_{r}\cdot nb_{r}$ , is a weighted sum of $nb_{r}$ ’s, with total weights $\delta_{r}$ ’s summing to $1$ .

### 2.3. Main Results on Relative Errors for Scaled Poisson Approximation

Consider the following notations adapted from [16]. Let $\pi_{k}=P(A_{\lambda}=k)=e^{-\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}$ , $k=0,1,\ldots$ , and

$$ \displaystyle F(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\pi_{k}\quad\mbox{ and }\quad{\overline{F}}(n)=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\pi_{k}. $$

Using the modified Stein’s operator (8), we establish the moderate deviations in the scaled Poisson approximation. Our main results are stated in the following theorems.

#### Theorem 2.1.

Consider a weighted Poisson sum $S=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}$ with integer weights $0<b_{1}<b_{2}<...<b_{R}$ , mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ . Let $\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}$ and $\lambda=\beta\mu$ , and $\delta_{r}=\frac{b_{r}\nu_{r}}{\mu}$ , $r=1,...,R$ . Assume $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\beta$ satisfies Assumption 1. Then, for all integers $y>\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{P(\beta S\geq y)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}-1\Bigg|\leq(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)+(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)+\alpha^{*} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle{\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda) \displaystyle:=\frac{\lambda+1}{y\pi_{y-1}} \displaystyle{\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda) \displaystyle:=\frac{2\lambda}{\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}\}}. $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{*}=\sum_{r=r^{*}+1}^{R}(\lceil\beta b_{r}\rceil-2)\delta_{r},\quad\mbox{with }r^{*}:=\max\{r:\beta b_{r}\leq 1,r=1,...,R\}. $$

The proof of Theorem 2.1 will be postponed to Sec. 3. Next, we show that the above relative bound also holds when $\beta$ is irrational.

#### Corollary 1.

Consider a weighted Poisson sum $S=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}$ with integer weights $0<b_{1}<b_{2}<...<b_{R}$ , mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ . Let $\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}$ and $\lambda=\beta\mu$ , and $\delta_{r}=\frac{b_{r}\nu_{r}}{\mu}$ , $r=1,...,R$ . Assume $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ . Then, (15) holds for all integers $y>\lambda+1$ .

#### Proof.

If $\beta$ is rational, then there is nothing to prove. If $\beta$ is irrational, then there is a sequence of rational numbers $\beta_{n},n=1,2,\ldots,\infty$ , satisfying $\beta_{n}<\beta$ and $\beta_{n}\rightarrow\beta$ , as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . For each $\beta_{n}$ , Theorem 2.1 implies that,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{P(\beta_{n}S\geq y)}{P(A_{\lambda_{n}}\geq y)}-1\Bigg|\leq(1+\alpha_{n}^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)+(1+\alpha_{n}^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)+\alpha_{n}^{*} $$

with $\lambda_{n}=\beta_{n}\mu$ , and,

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{n}^{*}=\sum_{r=r_{n}^{*}+1}^{R}(\lceil\beta_{n}b_{r}\rceil-2)\delta_{r},\quad\mbox{with }r_{n}^{*}:=\max\{r:\beta_{n}b_{r}\leq 1,r=1,...,R\}. $$

The assumption $\beta_{n}<\beta$ implies that $r_{n}^{*}\geq r^{*}$ , which leads to $\alpha^{*}_{n}\leq\alpha^{*}$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{P(\beta_{n}S\geq y)}{P(A_{\lambda_{n}}\geq y)}-1\Bigg|\leq(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)+(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)+\alpha^{*} $$

It is also easy to see that, as a consequence of the bounded convergence theorem,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}P(\beta_{n}S\geq y)=P(\beta S\geq y),\quad\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}P(A_{\lambda_{n}}\geq y)=P(A_{\lambda}\geq y). $$

Inequality (15) thus follows. ∎

The next theorem presents our main result in its final form, where all requirements in Assumption 1 are removed. That is, our relative error bound also holds for non-integer or irrational $b_{r}$ ’s.

#### Theorem 2.2 (Main Result).

Consider a weighted Poisson sum $S=\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}$ with weights $0<b_{1}<b_{2}<...<b_{R}$ , mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ . Let $\beta=\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}$ and $\lambda=\beta\mu$ , and $\delta_{r}=\frac{b_{r}\nu_{r}}{\mu}$ , $r=1,...,R$ . Assume $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ . Then, (15) holds for all integers $y>\lambda+1$ .

#### Proof.

First, consider the case that $b_{1},\ldots b_{R}$ are all rationals. We can find a large enough integer $B$ such that $b_{r}=\frac{\hat{b}_{r}}{B}$ , and $\hat{b}_{r}$ ’s are all integers, for $r=1,...,R$ . Let

$$ \hat{\mu}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat{b}_{r}\nu_{r},\quad\quad\hat{\sigma}^{2}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat{b}_{r}^{2}\nu_{r}. $$

We then have, $\mu=\frac{\hat{\mu}}{B},\sigma^{2}=\frac{\hat{\sigma}^{2}}{B^{2}}$ , and ${\beta}=B\hat{\beta}$ , $\lambda=\beta\mu=\hat{\beta}\hat{\mu}=\hat{\lambda}$ . Therefore, showing $S\approx_{d}\frac{1}{\beta}A_{\beta\mu}$ is equivalent to showing that $\hat{S}\approx_{d}\frac{1}{\hat{\beta}}A_{{\hat{\beta}}{\hat{\mu}}}$ , where $\hat{S}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat{b}_{r}A_{\nu_{r}}$ now satisfies that conditions of Corollary 1, with all the weights being positive integers.

If some of $b_{r}$ ’s are irrational, then there is a sequence of rational $R$ -tuples $(b_{r}^{(n)})_{r=1,\ldots,R}$ such that $b_{r}^{(n)}\leq b_{r}$ , for all $n=1,2,\ldots,\infty$ and $b_{r}^{(n)}\rightarrow b_{r}$ , as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . For each $n$ , Corollary 1 implies that,

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{P(S\geq y)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}-1\Bigg|\leq(1+\alpha_{(n)}^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)+(1+\alpha_{(n)}^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)+\alpha_{(n)}^{*} $$

with

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{(n)}^{*}=\sum_{r=r_{(n)}^{*}+1}^{R}(\lceil\beta b^{(n)}_{r}\rceil-2)\delta_{r},\quad\mbox{with }r_{(n)}^{*}:=\max\{r:\beta_{n}b^{(n)}_{r}\leq 1,r=1,...,R\}. $$

The assumption $b_{r}^{(n)}\leq b_{r}$ implies that $r_{(n)}^{*}\geq r^{*}$ , which leads to $\alpha^{*}_{(n)}\leq\alpha^{*}$ . Inequality (15) thus follows. ∎

#### Remark 2.1.

Theorem 2.2 indicates that the relative error of the scaled Poisson approximation depends on two main quantities of ${\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ . They are similar to the quantities ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{2}(\lambda,k)$ in [16] which play crucial roles in bounding the norm of the differences of the solution to the Stein equation for a Poisson approximation. The numerical results below demonstrate that ${\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ are comparable to, and in many cases smaller than, ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{2}(\lambda,k)$ . This confirms the power of Stein method in obtaining moderate deviations results for approximation of Poisson type.

In [16], ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{2}(\lambda,k)$ are compared to a“naive” counterpart $(1-e^{-\lambda})/(\lambda P(A_{\lambda}\geq k))$ , which bounds the absolute error of the Poisson approximation by $(1-e^{-\lambda})/\lambda$ through total variation analysis that can be found in [3], [1], and [4]. The same comparison can be carried out for ${\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ . More specifically, consider two groups of ratios:

$$ \text{ratio }+:={\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)/[(1-e^{-\lambda})/(\lambda P(A_{\lambda}\geq y))] $$

$$ \text{ratio }-:={\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)/[(1-e^{-\lambda})/(\lambda P(A_{\lambda}\geq y))] $$

for $y\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ ; and

$$ \text{ratio }i:={\mathfrak{C}}_{i}(\lambda,k)/[(1-e^{-\lambda})/(\lambda P(A_{\lambda}\geq k))],\quad i=1,2, $$

for $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , where ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{2}(\lambda,k)$ were defined in [16], with

$$ \displaystyle{\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k)= \displaystyle\frac{F(k-1)}{k\pi_{k}}\left(1-\frac{{\overline{F}}(k+1)}{{\overline{F}}(k)}\cdot\frac{k}{\lambda}\right), \displaystyle{\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)= \displaystyle\frac{F(k-1)}{k\pi_{k}}\left(1-\frac{F(k-2)}{F(k-1)}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{k-1}\right), $$

and whose maximum and summation are ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{2}(\lambda,k)$ , respectively.

#### Example 1.

Figure 1 demonstrates the two groups of ratios as a function of the tail parameter $y$ for the following 2-class example. Consider $S=A_{\nu_{1}}+2A_{\nu_{2}}$ with $\nu_{1}=1$ and $\nu_{2}=2$ . In this case, $b_{1}=1$ , $b_{2}=2$ , and $R=2$ . Based on (6), we have $\mu=5$ , $\sigma^{2}=9$ , and $\beta=5/9$ . Note that $\beta$ is a rational number with $n=5$ and $m=9$ that are relatively prime. Furthermore, we have $\lambda=\beta\mu=25/9$ .

Based on (18), we have $r^{*}=1$ and $\alpha^{*}=0$ . Thus the relative error bound (15) becomes:

$$ \displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{P(\beta S\geq y)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}-1\Bigg|\leq{\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)+{\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda) $$

As shown in the figure, both of our ratios (ratio + and ratio -) perform at similar scale as ratios 1 and 2 in [16], relative to the ”naive” counterparts. Note that ratios $1$ and $2$ are Poisson approximation that defined only on Poisson grid of $\hat{A}_{\lambda}(=mA_{\lambda})$ . Therefore, in the figure, we only have ratios defined for $y$ ’s that are divisible by $m$ , i.e., $k=\lfloor\frac{y}{m}\rfloor$ in (22) and (23).

The following corollary is immediate. It is easily checked from (16) and (17).

#### Corollary 2.

We have

$$ {\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)>{\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda),\quad\mbox{when $y$ is large.} $$

That is, the relative error bound (15) will eventually be dominated by ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ when $y$ is large enough.

### 2.4. On a conjecture in [16]

In [16], in an effort to establish moderate deviations for (non-scaled) Poisson approximations, the authors show that the Stein method is reduced to the evaluation of the two quantities, ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k)$ , which are defined in (23) and (22), respectively.

In [16], it was conjectured that (Conjecture 4.2)

$$ {\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)>{\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k), $$

thus ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)$ plays a dominant role in their error bounds for the non-scaled Poisson approximation.

The next proposition shows that the above conjecture is indeed true when $k$ is large enough and further provides the specific threshold on $k$ . The detailed proof can be found in Appendix H.

#### Proposition 1.

When $k\geq(\lambda+1)+\sqrt{(\lambda+1)(5\lambda+1)}$ , we have,

$$ {\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)>{\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k), $$

where ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)$ are defined in (22) and (23), respectively. That is, the moderate deviation results of [16] can be rewritten in terms of ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1+}(\lambda,k)$ , and the relative error bound will be eventually dominated by ${\mathfrak{C}}_{1-}(\lambda,k)$ for large $k$ .

## 3. Proof of Theorem 2.1

Let

$$ h(w)=\mathbb{I}\{w:w\geq my\},\quad\mbox{ for }w\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. $$

Let $f_{h}$ be the solution to Stein’s equation (9) with $h$ given by (26). Since $E[h(nS)]=P(nS\geq my)$ , we have

$$ P(nS\geq my)-P(\hat{A}_{\lambda}\geq my)=Eh(nS)-Eh({\hat{A}}_{\lambda})=E\mathcal{A}f_{h}(nS). $$

Apply Lemma 2.4 to equation (27), we have:

$$ P(nS\geq my)-P(\hat{A}_{\lambda}\geq my)=H_{1}+\cdots+H_{R}, $$

where $H_{r}$ is defined in (12). Therefore, to bound the deviation between the tail distributions of $nS$ and $\hat{A}_{\lambda}$ , it suffices to bound $|H_{1}|$ , $\cdots$ , and $|H_{R}|$ .

The next lemma provides important bounds on differences of $f_{h}$ which will be useful in bounding $|H_{r}|$ ’s. It depends on a sequence of lemmas (Lemmas 4.1-4.12) that reveal the key properties of function $f_{h}$ which are presented in section 4. The proof of Lemma 3.1 is provided at the end of section 4.

#### Lemma 3.1.

For all integers $y\geq\lambda+1$ , we have:

$$ \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS)|]\leq P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\left[{B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y)\right], $$

and for $0<\ell<m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+\ell)|]\leq P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\left[{B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\right], $$

where

$$ \displaystyle{B}_{+}(y) \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda my\pi_{y-1}} \displaystyle{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y) \displaystyle=\frac{2}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}}\}+\frac{1}{m\lambda}, \displaystyle{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y) \displaystyle=\frac{2}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}\}}. $$

The next lemma presents bounds on the $|H_{r}|$ ’s.

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $r^{*}=\max\{r:\beta b_{r}\leq 1,r=1,...,R\}$ , and $K_{r}=\lceil\beta b_{r}\rceil$ .

- • For $1\leq r\leq r^{*}$ , we have (34) $\displaystyle|H_{r}|\leq P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot\delta_{r}\lambda m\left[{B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\right];$

- • For $r>r^{*}$ , we have (35) $\displaystyle|H_{r}|\leq P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot\delta_{r}\lambda m\left[\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\Big)+(K_{r}-2)\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y)\Big)\right].$

#### Proof.

Since $\beta=n/m$ , $\{\beta b_{r}\leq 1\}\Longleftrightarrow\{nb_{r}\leq m\}$ .

Thus, $r^{*}=\max\{r:\beta b_{r}\leq 1,r=1,...,R\}$ is simply the largest $r$ that satisfies $nb_{r}\leq m$ ; and for all $r=r^{*}+1,...,R$ , we have $nb_{r}>m$ and $K_{r}=\lceil\beta b_{r}\rceil\geq 2$ .

For $1\leq r\leq r^{*}$ , since $nb_{r}\leq m$ , we have $0\leq\Delta=m-nb_{r}<m$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle|H_{r}|= \displaystyle\lambda m\delta_{r}E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+nb_{r})| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\lambda m\delta_{r}P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\left[{B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\right], $$

where the inequality follows from Lemma 3.1.

For $r=r^{*}+1,...,R$ , since $nb_{r}>m$ , the gap between $nS+m$ and $nS+nb_{r}$ may contain multiple $m$ -steps. Since $K_{r}-1<\beta b_{r}\leq K_{r}$ , and $\beta=\frac{n}{m}$ , we have $(K_{r}-1)m<nb_{r}\leq K_{r}m$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle|H_{r}|= \displaystyle\lambda m\delta_{r}E[|f_{h}(nS+nb_{r})-f_{h}(nS+m)|] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\lambda m\delta_{r}E[|f_{h}(nS+nb_{r})-f_{h}(nS+(K_{r}-1)m)|+\ldots \displaystyle\hskip 198.7425pt+|f_{h}(nS+2m)-f_{h}(nS+m)|] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot\lambda m\delta_{r}\left[\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\Big)+(K_{r}-2)\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y)\Big)\right] $$

where the last inequality is due to Lemma 3.1.

∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 2.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.1.

Based on (28) and Lemma 3.2, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\frac{P[nS\geq my]}{P[{A}_{\lambda}\geq y]}-1\Big| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{r^{*}}|H_{r}|+\sum_{r=r^{*}+1}^{R}|H_{r}|}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{r^{*}}\delta_{r}\lambda m\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\Big) \displaystyle+\sum_{r=r^{*}+1}^{R}\delta_{r}\lambda m\left[\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\Big)+(K_{r}-2)\Big({B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y)\Big)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\Big(1+\sum_{r^{*}+1}^{R}(K_{r}-2)\delta_{r}\Big)\lambda m{B}_{+}(y))+\lambda m{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)+\Big(\sum_{r^{*}+1}^{R}(K_{r}-2)\delta_{r}\Big)\lambda m{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+\alpha^{*})\lambda m\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda my\pi_{y-1}}+\frac{2\lambda m}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}\}}+\alpha^{*}\lambda m\Big[\frac{2}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}}\}+\frac{1}{m\lambda}\Big] \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+\alpha^{*})\frac{\lambda+1}{y\pi_{y-1}}+(1+\alpha^{*})\frac{2\lambda}{\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}\}}+\alpha^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda))+(1+\alpha^{*}){\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)+\alpha^{*} $$

where $\alpha^{*}$ is defined by (18), and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ by (16) and (17) respectively. Theorem 2.1 therefore follows. ∎

## 4. Properties of the Solution to the Stein Equation

In this section, we present a sequence of lemmas that provide important properties of function $f_{h}$ , the solution to the Stein’s equation, which are essential to the proof of Lemma 3.1.

### 4.1. Some Basic Properties of $f_{h}$

Recall that for $h(w)=\mathbb{I}\{w:w\geq my\}$ , where $w\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , Lemma 2.2 states that $f_{h}$ , the solution to the Stein’s equation, takes the following form:

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w)=-\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}[h(w+mj)-P({\hat{A}}_{\lambda}\geq my)]. $$

Define $k_{w}:=\lceil\frac{(my-w)^{+}}{m}\rceil$ . Equivalently, $k_{w}=\inf\{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},w+km\geq my\}$ , i.e. $k_{w}$ is the minimum number of $m$ -jumps, starting from $w$ , to reach or go above $my$ (i.e. $\geq my$ ). When $w\geq my$ , $k_{w}=0$ naturally. Therefore, $h(w+mj)=\mathbb{I}\{j\geq k_{w}\}$ . Moreover, $P({\hat{A}}_{\lambda}\geq my)=P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)$ . Thus (36) can be rewritten as,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w)= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}-\sum_{j=k_{w}}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}. $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(k,w):=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)},\qquad\overline{\Theta}(k,w):=\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)},\qquad\mbox{ for $k\geq 0$} $$

(37) can then be rewritten as follows:

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w)= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\overline{\Theta}(0,w)-\overline{\Theta}(k_{w},w) $$

The next lemma provides an important relation between $f_{h}(w+m)$ and $f_{h}(w)$ .

#### Lemma 4.1.

For all $w\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w+m)=\frac{w}{\lambda m}f_{h}(w)-\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)-1_{w\geq my}}{\lambda m} $$

or, equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle Df_{h}(w):=f_{h}(w+m)-f_{h}(w)= \displaystyle f_{h}(w)\left(\frac{w}{\lambda m}-1\right)-\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)-1_{w\geq my}}{\lambda m}. $$

#### Proof.

If $w\geq my$ , then $k_{w}=0$ and $k_{w+m}=0$ . Then, (37) becomes

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w+m) \displaystyle=-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m(\ell+1))} \displaystyle=-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j+1}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j+1}(w+m\ell)}\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m} \displaystyle=-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\left[\sum_{j^{\prime}=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j^{\prime}}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j^{\prime}}(w+m\ell)}-\frac{1}{w}\right]\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m} \displaystyle=\frac{w}{\lambda m}f_{h}(w)+\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}<y)}{\lambda m} $$

If $w<my$ , then $k_{w}=\lceil\frac{my-w}{m}\rceil\geq 1$ , and $k_{w+m}=k_{w}-1$ . Then (37) becomes

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w+m) \displaystyle= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m+m\ell)}-\sum_{j=k_{w}-1}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m+m\ell)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j+1}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j+1}(w+m\ell)}\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m}-\sum_{j=k_{w}-1}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j+1}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j+1}(w+m\ell)}\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m} \displaystyle= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\left[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}-\frac{1}{w}\right]\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m}-\sum_{j=k_{w}}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}\cdot\frac{w}{\lambda m} \displaystyle= \displaystyle f_{h}(w)\left(\frac{w}{\lambda m}\right)-\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}{\lambda m}. $$

In both cases, equation (40) is satisfied. ∎

The following lemma will be useful in deriving bounds. The proof is in Appendix D.

#### Lemma 4.2.

For any integer $k\geq 0$ , we have:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{m\lambda\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor}}P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq k+\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor+1\right]\leq{\overline{\Theta}(k,w)} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\max(1,\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor)\cdot m\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor}}P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq k+\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor\right]. $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{m\lambda\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor}}P\left(\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor+1\leq A_{\lambda}\leq k+\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor+1\right)\leq{{\Theta}(k,w)} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\max(1,\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor)\cdot m\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor}}P\left(\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor\leq A_{\lambda}\leq k+\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor\right). $$

The following two lemmas provide some useful results on Poisson probabilities.

#### Lemma 4.3.

For any Poisson r.v. $A_{\lambda}$ with $\lambda>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{P(A_{\lambda}\geq k+1)}{P(A_{\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\geq}k)} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\lambda}{k+1},\mbox{ for any $k>\lambda-1$} \displaystyle\frac{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y+k)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\lambda}{y+k},\mbox{ for any $k\geq 1$, and $y\geq\lambda$} $$

#### Proof.

It has been observed in [10] that

$$ \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}\geq k)= \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}=k)(1+\frac{\lambda}{k+1}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{(k+1)(k+2)}+...) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}=k)(1+\frac{\lambda}{k+1}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{(k+1)^{2}}+...) \displaystyle= \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}=k)\frac{k+1}{k-\lambda+1}\quad\mbox{ for all $k>\lambda-1$.} $$

Thus, (44) follows noting that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{P(A_{\lambda}\geq k+1)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq k)}=1-\frac{P(A_{\lambda}=k)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq k)}\leq 1-\frac{k-\lambda+1}{k+1}=\frac{\lambda}{k+1}. $$

To show (45), we apply (44) to $y+k-1$ , for any $k\geq 1$ and $y\geq\lambda$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}\geq y+k)\leq\frac{\lambda}{y+k}P(A_{\lambda}\geq y+k-1)\leq\frac{\lambda}{y+k}P(A_{\lambda}\geq y) $$

∎

It is well known that the mode of Poisson distribution is $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$ for non-integer $\lambda$ . When $\lambda$ is a positive integer, the modes are $\lambda$ and $\lambda-1$ . Furthermore, the Poisson probabilities are increasing before the mean value $\lambda$ and decreasing after $\lambda$ .

#### Lemma 4.4.

For any Poisson r.v. $A_{\lambda}$ with $\lambda>0$ and $\pi_{k}=P(A_{\lambda}=k)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\pi_{k}}{\pi_{k-1}} \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{k},\quad\quad\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$; }, \displaystyle\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1} \displaystyle\geq\frac{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}{\lambda}\pi_{y-2},\quad\mbox{for $m\lambda\leq w<my$, where $y$ is an integer and $y>\lambda+1$.} $$

#### Proof.

(46) can be easily verified using the definition of $\pi_{k}$ .

If $\lambda<1$ , (47) is immediate since $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor=0$ .

Now suppose $\lambda\geq 1$ . Since $m\lambda\leq w<my$ , we have $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\leq\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor\leq y-1$ and $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor-1\leq\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1\leq y-2$ .

If $\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1\geq\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$ , then (47) is immediate since $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$ is the mode and the Poisson probabilities are decreasing after the mean value $\lambda$ .

If $\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1=\lfloor\lambda\rfloor-1$ , then

$$ \pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1}=\pi_{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor-1}=\pi_{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}\frac{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}{\lambda}\geq\frac{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}{\lambda}\pi_{y-2}, $$

where the second equality is due to (46), and the last inequality is because $y-2\geq\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$ since $y-1>\lambda$ and $y$ is an integer.

∎

We next analyze the behavior of $f_{h}(w)$ for the cases of $w\geq my$ and $w<my$ separately.

### 4.2. The Case of $w\geq my$

For $w\geq my$ , observe that $h(w+mj)=1$ for all integer $j\geq 0$ , and $P({\hat{A}}_{\lambda}<my)=P({A}_{\lambda}<y)$ , thus,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w)=-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)},\mbox{ for }w\geq my. $$

The following lemma is immediate.

#### Lemma 4.5.

For $w\geq my$ , $f_{h}(w)<0$ and $f_{h}(w)$ is monotonically increasing and concave in $w$ .

#### Proof.

It is easy to verify that each summand in (48)

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)} $$

is decreasing and convex with respect to $w$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.1.

Lemma 4.5 tells us that the differences of the Stein function, the key quantities in our study, are non-negative and decreasing in $w$ . Hence, to estimate the maximum value they can achieve, only the first of them needs to be evaluated, for $w\geq my$ .

#### Lemma 4.6.

For $w\geq my$ , we have,

$$ 0\leq\frac{f_{h}(w+l)-f_{h}(w)}{l}\leq P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda m^{2}y\pi_{y-1}}\quad\mbox{ for all $l>0$}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $f_{h}(w)$ is increasing and concave for $w\geq my$ , we have, for all $l>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{f_{h}(w+l)-f_{h}(w)}{l}\leq\frac{d}{dw}f_{h}(w)\Big|_{w=my}=P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(my+m\ell)}\sum_{k=0}^{j}\frac{1}{my+mk}. $$

where the RHS is because

$$ \frac{d}{dw}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}=-\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}\sum_{k=0}^{j}\frac{1}{w+mk}. $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{j}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(my+m\ell)}\frac{1}{(my+mk)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(my+m\ell)}\frac{1}{(my+mk)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{my+mk}\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(my+m\ell)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(y+\ell)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{j+y}}{(y+j)!}\cdot\frac{(y-1)!}{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\lambda m^{2}\pi_{y-1}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}P(A_{\lambda}\geq y+k) $$

Based on (45), we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}\frac{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y+k)}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{1}{y}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{y+k}\leq\frac{1}{y}+\lambda(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}-\frac{1}{y+k+1})\leq\frac{\lambda+1}{y}. $$

Combine with (49), we then have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{f_{h}(w+l)-f_{h}(w)}{l\cdot P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}<y)}{\lambda m^{2}\pi_{y-1}}\cdot\frac{\lambda+1}{y}\leq\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda m^{2}y\pi_{y-1}} $$

∎

#### Remark 4.2.

Note that (50) can be written as:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{my+mk}\overline{\Theta}(k,my) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m(y+k)}\cdot\frac{1}{y\cdot m\pi_{y}}P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq y+k\right]\quad\mbox{(based on \eqref{eqn:barTheta} with $w=my$ and $\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor=y$)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m(y+k)}\cdot\frac{1}{m\lambda\pi_{y-1}}P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq y+k\right]\quad\mbox{(since $y\pi_{y}=\lambda\pi_{y-1}$)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\lambda m^{2}\pi_{y-1}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{y+k}\cdot P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq y+k\right] $$

Note that (52) is identical as (51), which indicates that the upper bound given by (42) is tight for $w=my$ .

### 4.3. The Case of $w<my$

When $w<my$ , $k_{w}\geq 1$ . Note that we can rewrite (37) as:

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w) \displaystyle=P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\sum_{j=0}^{k_{w}-1}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\sum_{j=k_{w}}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)},\quad\forall k_{w}\geq 1. $$

Or equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w)= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\Theta(k_{w}-1,w)-P({A}_{\lambda}<y)\overline{\Theta}(k_{w},w), $$

#### Lemma 4.7.

For any $m\lambda\leq w<my$ , $Df_{h}(w)=f_{h}(w+m)-f_{h}(w)<0$ . That is, $f_{h}(w)$ is decreasing on the $m$ -grid.

#### Proof.

If $k_{w}=1$ , we have $w+m\geq my$ and $w<my$ . Based on Lemma 4.1, from (40), we have $f_{h}(w)=\frac{\lambda m}{w}f_{h}(w+m)+\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}{w}$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w+m)-f_{h}(w)=(1-\frac{\lambda m}{w})f(w+m)-\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}{w}<0, $$

where the inequality is because $f(w+m)<0$ based on Lemma 4.5.

Now consider the case $k_{w}\geq 2$ . Based on (53) and $k_{w+m}=k_{w}-1$ , it is easy to verify that,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(w+m)-f_{h}(w)= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\sum_{j=0}^{k_{w}-2}\left[\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m+m\ell)}-\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}\right] \displaystyle-P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\frac{(\lambda m)^{k_{w}-1}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{k_{w}-1}(w+m\ell)} \displaystyle-(\frac{w}{\lambda m}-1)\sum_{j=k_{w}}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda m)^{j}}{\prod_{\ell=0}^{j}(w+m\ell)}[1-P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)]<0, $$

where the first two terms are obviously negative, and the last term is negative since $m\lambda\leq w<my$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.8.

For $m\lambda\leq w<my$ , for any $j=1,...,k_{w}-1$ , where $k_{w}=\lceil\frac{(my-w)}{m}\rceil$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle D_{h}(w+jm)-D_{h}(w+(j-1)m)\leq P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot T_{m}(y), $$

where $T_{m}(y)=\frac{1}{m\lambda{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}\pi_{y-2}}$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $k_{w}=\lceil\frac{(my-w)}{m}\rceil$ is the minimum number of $m$ -jumps required to reach or go above $my$ starting from $w$ . Hence, $k_{w}\geq 1$ , $w+(k_{w}-1)m<my$ , and $w+k_{w}m\geq my$ . For any $j=1,...,k_{w}-1$ , we have $w\leq w+(j-1)m<w+jm<my$ .

Apply (41) of Lemma 4.1 to both $w+(j-1)m$ and $w+jm$ , we have,

$$ \displaystyle Df_{h}(w+jm)]-Df_{h}(w+(j-1)m) \displaystyle= \displaystyle f_{h}(w+jm)\left(\frac{w+jm}{\lambda m}-1\right)-f_{h}(w+(j-1)m)\left(\frac{w+(j-1)m}{\lambda m}-1\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle[f_{h}(w+jm)-f_{h}(w+(j-1)m)]\left(\frac{w+jm}{\lambda m}-1\right)+\frac{f_{h}(w+(j-1)m)}{\lambda} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{f_{h}(w)}{\lambda}\quad\quad\mbox{(since $f_{h}(w+jm)$ is decreasing on the m-grid)} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot\overline{\Theta}(0,w)}{\lambda}\quad\mbox{(based on \eqref{eqn:SteinEq5})} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}{\lambda}\frac{P\left[A_{\lambda}\geq\left\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\right\rfloor\right]}{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor m\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor}}\quad\mbox{(based on \eqref{eqn:barTheta}) and
$1\leq\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\leq\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor$)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\frac{1}{m\lambda^{2}\pi_{\lfloor\frac{w}{m}\rfloor-1}}\quad\mbox{(since $k\pi_{k}=\lambda\pi_{k-1}$)} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)\frac{1}{m\lambda{\lfloor\lambda\rfloor}\pi_{y-2}} $$

where the second to last inequality is due to (42), and the last inequality is due to (47). ∎

The following three lemmas are important for the proof of the main theorem. The proofs are available in the Appendix.

#### Lemma 4.9.

For $w<\lambda m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|f_{h}(w)-f_{h}(w+m)|}{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{1}{m\pi_{0}}+\frac{1}{m\lambda}. $$

The proof of Lemma 4.9 can be found in Appendix E.

#### Lemma 4.10.

For $m\lambda\leq w<my$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\frac{f_{h}(w)-f_{h}(w+m)}{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{2}{m\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}}+\frac{1}{my}(\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda}). $$

The proof of Lemma 4.10 can be found in Appendix F.

Combine the above two lemmas we then have the following result.

#### Lemma 4.11.

For $w<my$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|f_{h}(w+m)-f_{h}(w)|}{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{2}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}}\}+\frac{1}{m\lambda}=:{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y) $$

#### Lemma 4.12.

For $w<my$ , we have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|f_{h}(w+d)-f_{h}(w)|}{P({A}_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq\frac{2}{m\cdot\min\{\pi_{0},\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\pi_{y-1}\}}=:{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y),\quad\mbox{for $d=1,2,\ldots,m-1$.} $$

The proof of Lemma 4.12 can be found in Appendix G.

We are now ready to prove Lemma 3.1.

#### Proof.

(Proof of Lemma 3.1) Based on Lemma 4.6, we know that, for any $l=0,1,...,m-1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+\ell)|{\bf 1}_{nS+\ell\geq my}]}{P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)}\leq(m-l)\cdot\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda m^{2}y\pi_{y-1}}\leq\frac{\lambda+1}{\lambda my\pi_{y-1}}=:{B}_{+}(y). $$

(29) follows noting that

$$ \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS)|] \displaystyle= \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS)|\cdot{\bf 1}_{nS\geq my}]+E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS)|\cdot{\bf 1}_{nS<my}] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot{{B}_{+}(y)}+P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\cdot{B}^{(m)}_{-}(y). $$

where the inequality is due to (60) and Lemma 4.11.

(30) follows because

$$ \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+\ell)|] \displaystyle= \displaystyle E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+\ell)|({\bf 1}_{nS+\ell\geq my}]+E[|f_{h}(nS+m)-f_{h}(nS+\ell)|{\bf 1}_{nS+\ell<my})] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle P(A_{\lambda}\geq y)\left[{B}_{+}(y)+{B}^{(d)}_{-}(y)\right], $$

where the inequality is due to (60) and Lemma 4.12. ∎

## 5. Conclusions

In this paper, we derive bounds on the relative error of a scaled Poisson approximation to the weighted sum of independent Poisson random variables via a modified Stein’s method. While our proof techniques require the studies of a new Stein’s operator that acts on the grid $mZ_{\geq 0}$ when $\beta$ is a rational number $\beta=\frac{n}{m}$ , our final result does not rely on the rational assumption. We show that the relative error of the approximation is essentially bounded by two main quantities ${\mathfrak{C}}_{+}(y;\lambda)$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{-}(y;\lambda)$ . The ratios of these two quantities relative to the naive bound perform at similar scale as the ratios in [16] in the non-scaled Poisson approximation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that one of the conjectures raised in [16] is valid beyond a threshold that has an explicitly expression.
